realLife: Credit-risk, demand and sensor models often use small fully connected networks on tabular inputs.
summary: Stack neurons in layers with a bend between them and the model can draw curved boundaries.
headline: Layers turn lines into curves
overview: A hidden layer feeds the outputs of several simple neurons into the next one. With a bend, an activation function, between layers, the network can combine straight cuts into curved regions.
Without that bend, any number of layers collapses back into a single straight line. Width and depth decide how flexible the curve can be.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Remove every hidden layer and ask for two concentric rings. What is left is one straight line, so accuracy stays near a coin flip however long you train.

check.question: Why do hidden layers need a nonlinear activation?
options: Without one, stacked layers equal a single linear model
It removes the need for data

data: One hundred and sixty points from four shapes, centred to the range -1 to 1, split 70/30. Training uses Adam at a fixed learning rate. Results depend on the random start, so a different seed can shift the numbers a little.
maths: If φ is the identity, then W⁽²⁾W⁽¹⁾ is just another matrix and the network is a linear classifier again. The nonlinearity is what makes depth useful.
code:
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
m = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(8, 8), activation='tanh', max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
